cases.task: Implement mergeIntervals(intervals) as a JavaScript function expression. Intervals are finite numeric half-open [start,end] pairs with end>=start. Return sorted merged intervals, merge touching boundaries, ignore zero-length intervals, support unsorted/nested/duplicate and negative coordinates, and do not mutate input. No imports or side effects. Return JSON only {"artifact":"function mergeIntervals(intervals){...}"}.

baseline.artifact: function mergeIntervals(intervals){const cleaned=[];for(let i=0;i<intervals.length;i++){const s=intervals[i][0],e=intervals[i][1];if(e>s)cleaned.push([s,e]);}cleaned.sort((a,b)=>a[0]-b[0]||a[1]-b[1]);const merged=[];for(const [s,e] of cleaned){if(merged.length===0){merged.push([s,e]);continue;}const last=merged[merged.length-1];if(s<=last[1]){if(e>last[1])last[1]=e;}else{merged.push([s,e]);}}return merged;}

revised.artifact: function mergeIntervals(intervals){const cleaned=[];for(let i=0;i<intervals.length;i++){const s=intervals[i][0],e=intervals[i][1];if(e>s)cleaned.push([s,e]);}cleaned.sort((a,b)=>a[0]-b[0]||a[1]-b[1]);const merged=[];for(const [s,e] of cleaned){if(merged.length===0){merged.push([s,e]);continue;}const last=merged[merged.length-1];if(s<=last[1]){if(e>last[1])last[1]=e;}else{merged.push([s,e]);}}return merged;}

report.summary: The current draft satisfies every stated requirement of the original task: zero-length intervals are dropped (e>s), touching half-open boundaries merge (s<=last[1]), output is start-sorted, nested/duplicate/negative inputs work, and input is never mutated (new [s,e] arrays are pushed and only those copies are updated). Traced [[1,4],[2,3],[5,7],[6,8]]→[[1,4],[5,8]] and [[1,2],[1,2]]→[[1,2]] both correct. No substantive gain found over the current text.
assumptions: Input elements are always well-formed [start,end] numeric pairs with end>=start, as the task states; no malformed-input handling is required and none is added.

findings.text: Zero-length filtering uses e>s; since the spec guarantees end>=start, this is exactly 'drop when end===start' with no valid interval lost.
Merge condition s<=last[1] correctly implements touching-boundary merging for half-open intervals; nested intervals are handled by the e>last[1] guard and duplicates collapse.
Non-mutation holds because only freshly constructed [s,e] arrays enter cleaned/merged; the sort and last[1]=e writes touch copies, not the caller's arrays.
Sort comparator a[0]-b[0]||a[1]-b[1] is numeric and safe for negative coordinates; the secondary end-key is harmless though not strictly required.

cases.task: Analyze success rates for method A versus B. Easy group: A 81 successes of 90, B 234 of 270. Hard group: A 192 of 240, B 55 of 75. Explain the pooled-versus-group relationship and whether the pooled result alone supports choosing B; keep the explanation within 180 words, distinguish description from causal conclusions. Return JSON {"artifact":"analysis","metrics":{"easyA":number,"easyB":number,"hardA":number,"hardB":number,"pooledA":number,"pooledB":number},"decision":"A|B|insufficient"}. Rates must be proportions.

baseline.explanation: Easy: A 0.900 vs B 0.867; hard: A 0.800 vs B 0.733. A has higher observed success in both groups. Pooled: A 0.827 vs B 0.838, so B appears higher only when groups are combined. This reversal is Simpson's paradox: B's pooled rate is boosted because 78% of B cases are easy (270/345), while only 55% of A cases are easy (90/330); easy cases have higher success. Pooled result alone therefore does not support choosing B; it is confounded by case-mix. Descriptively, the stratified rates favor A. Causal conclusion—that A causes better outcomes—requires assumptions such as no unmeasured confounding; these data alone do not prove causation. Decision uses descriptive within-group comparisons: A.

arguments.question:
Goal: a local (no server/DB-service) document index for a large mixed-format archive (many GB, hundreds of thousands of files, mixed text/PDF/office/binary), with three hard constraints: (1) bounded memory — must not load the corpus or a huge index into RAM; (2) frequent file updates — files are added/modified/deleted continuously, re-indexing must be incremental; (3) crash recovery — indexing is frequently interrupted and must resume correctly after a kill, without corruption or duplicated/stale entries. Deliverable is working Python code (single machine, stdlib + maybe one common dep) using SQLite as the candidate structure.

Decisions I need made concretely, since I have not locked these: (a) Is SQLite actually the right maintainable structure versus e.g. a directory of JSON/segment files with a manifest, or an append-only log + compaction? Give the trade-off and a definite pick. (b) Exact schema + WAL/pragma settings for bounded memory and concurrent read-during-write. (c) Exact crash-recovery semantics: what makes a file "done", how checkpoints/watermarks work, how to detect and redo files that were in-flight at crash time, and how to avoid marking a partially-indexed file as complete. (d) Incremental update detection that is cheap: mtime+size vs content hash, and how to avoid re-reading unchanged large files. (e) Mixed-format extraction that fails gracefully so one bad PDF doesn't abort the batch. (f) Batch/transaction granularity that keeps memory bounded and fsync cost sane. Return a specific recommended design with schema DDL, the indexing loop, and the recovery procedure.

Note: I want the design decided now and then implemented; I don't want an exhaustive survey. Prefer the smallest design that satisfies all three constraints.
arguments.hypothesis: Single SQLite file in WAL mode; one row per file with a status column (pending/done/error); per-file transactions committed in batches; journal_mode=WAL + synchronous=NORMAL; completion marked only after content rows are committed, so a crash leaves files in 'pending' and a resume pass re-scans them; incremental updates via mtime_ns+size fast-path with content hash to disambiguate.

rows.text: I'll lock down the design before writing code, since the structure choice (single SQLite file vs. append-only log vs. directory-of-files index) is consequential and hard to reverse.

arguments.focus: Local document index for a large mixed-format archive: bounded memory, frequent incremental updates, crash/interrupt recovery mid-index. Choosing the persistent structure and the checkpoint/journal protocol before implementing.
arguments.question: I need to pick a maintainable persistent index structure + recovery protocol for a local archive indexer. Constraints: (1) bounded memory regardless of archive size (millions of files, mixed formats: text, PDF, docx, images with sidecar text); (2) frequent updates — files added/changed/deleted continuously, so re-index must be incremental; (3) interrupted indexing must be recoverable without full re-scan and without corrupting the index; (4) it must be maintainable by one person (no server, no external service). Candidate: SQLite as single-file store with WAL + a per-batch checkpoint, streaming extraction in batches, and content-hash-based change detection. Questions I want an independent take on: Is SQLite the right backbone versus an append-only segment + compaction log (Lucene-style) or a plain directory-of-JSON-files index? What is the minimal correct recovery protocol — what exactly must be committed atomically per batch so that a crash leaves the index in a consistent state and progress can resume from the last completed batch? What are the specific failure modes I should design against (partial extraction, killed process mid-batch, file changed between hash and extract, duplicate inserts after resume)?
arguments.hypothesis: SQLite (WAL mode) as the index backbone, with one transaction per batch containing both document rows and a progress/checkpoint row, content hashes for change detection, and resume driven by the checkpoint table rather than by rescanning the archive.
